content.title: Chuck Norris net worth revealed: How the action icon built a $70 million fortune before his death
content.text: In 2025, gold delivered one of its strongest performances since 1979. A “perfect storm” of geopolitical tensions, central bank buying, and global policy shifts powered bullion to historic highs.The rally extended into 2026, with prices surging past $5,000 an ounce, delivering another year of double-digit returns.In 2025, US markets delivered a third consecutive year of double-digit gains, though the ride was significantly more volatile than previous years.The benchmark S&P 500 finished the year with a total return (including dividends) of 17.9%. The Nasdaq Composite was up more than 20%.For many Indian investors, this reignited a familiar debate: Should gold be the primary hedge in a portfolio—or is allocating 20–30% to U.S. equities a smarter long-term strategy?The answer begins with a simple truth: gold and equities serve fundamentally different purposes. Comparing them directly is often a category error.Gold: A Hedge, Not a Growth EngineGold has historically served as a store of value and a hedge against macro shocks. In India, a portion of gold’s long-term appreciation—roughly 25% of its growth—has come from rupee depreciation against the dollar.That works if your primary objective is to benefit from currency weakness. But portfolios are built to optimize overall returns, not just capture rupee depreciation.Over long cycles, gold does not compete with equities in terms of wealth creation. Its recent surge is also partly influenced by recency bias—driven by geopolitical tensions and safe-haven flows. Before the latest rally, gold’s annual returns were generally in single digits.And importantly, gold does not always hedge currency risk. During India’s 2013 rupee crisis—when the dollar moved from ₹54 to ₹68 in just a few months—gold fell 28% while the S&P 500 rose 32%. Investors holding only Indian equities and gold suffered in dollar terms. The episode proved that gold can sometimes amplify losses rather than cushion them. U.S. Equities: Diversified Growth & Currency AdvantageWhen comparing U.S. equities and Indian equities, we are comparing equity vs equity—a far more relevant framework.A U.S. allocation offers:4–5% potential annual tailwind from rupee depreciation, on top of underlying equity growthLow correlation with Indian equities, improving diversificationAccess to global sector leadershipConsider sector composition. The Nifty 50 is dominated by financials (36.5%) and traditional energy (14.7%)—over half the index. In contrast, the S&P 500 allocates about 30% to technology alone.The largest U.S. companies are leaders in sectors that are difficult to replicate domestically:Semiconductors, AI, cloud computing, biotech, energy transition, advanced manufacturing.Comparing a broad index to gold can also be misleading. Index returns include laggards. If one compares gold’s recent performance to just the “Magnificent 7” U.S. tech leaders, those stocks have decisively outperformed bullion over time.Limiting U.S. exposure to just 10–15% increases geographical concentration risk—something gold cannot hedge against.What About Gold ETFs and Gold Miners?For Indian investors who want gold exposure without physical ownership hassles, Gold ETFs remain one of the simplest routes.Globally, investors also access gold miner ETFs, which provide exposure to mining companies rather than bullion itself. These vehicles blend gold price exposure with equity characteristics.When gold prices rise, miners’ profitability can expand faster due to operating leverage—often amplifying returns.That dynamic was evident in 2025, when gold mining equities outperformed bullion as record prices boosted margins.However, Indian exchanges do not offer gold miner ETFs. Through global investing platforms like Appreciate, Indian investors can access international gold miner ETFs and broader U.S. equity markets—using them as higher-risk satellite allocations alongside core holdings.So, Gold or 20–30% U.S. Allocation?It is not an either/or decision.Gold plays the role of portfolio insurance—useful, stabilizing, but not a growth driver.U.S. equities offer structural growth, currency diversification, sector leadership, and lower correlation with Indian markets.In a world of rising globalization and innovation cycles, a 20–30% allocation to U.S. equities can meaningfully enhance long-term portfolio efficiency, while a measured gold allocation can provide tactical stability.The real question isn’t whether gold is a hedge. It is.The question is: Are you building a portfolio to protect wealth—or to grow it globally?With access to international markets through platforms like Appreciate, Indian investors no longer have to choose between domestic exposure and global opportunity. They can design portfolios that do both. (This article is generated and published by ET Spotlight team. You can get in touch with them on etspotlight@timesinternet.in)
